entities.summary:
Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points (HACCP) is a systematic preventive approach to food safety created by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) in the 1960s. HACCP aims to minimize the risk of foodborne illnesses by identifying and controlling potential hazards in food production processes. The approach is based on a risk-based system that evaluates the probability of contamination and takes corrective actions to prevent its occurrence. HACCP has become a widely adopted global standard for ensuring food safety and has played a crucial role in reducing foodborne illnesses worldwide. By applying HACCP principles, manufacturers can identify critical control points in their production processes and implement measures to prevent contamination, thereby protecting public health.

HACCP was first implemented in the 1960s by NASA's food technology department, which aimed to develop a reliable method for ensuring food safety during space missions. The approach was later adapted for use in the food industry and has since become a widely accepted standard for ensuring food safety. HACCP has been recognized as a key factor in reducing foodborne illnesses and improving public health.

The implementation of HACCP has had a significant impact on the food industry, leading to improved food safety practices and reduced risk of foodborne illnesses. HACCP has also enabled manufacturers to comply with food safety regulations and has become a cornerstone of food safety management systems.
